topic: Peptides your body makes / discovery story: PTH (parathyroid hormone), the calcium controller made by 4 small glands behind the thyroid. 4 small glands posterior to the thyroid; PTH is an 84-amino-acid polypeptide released when blood calcium drops, high calcium stops release (negative feedback); bone: releases calcium via osteoclasts; kidney: increases calcium reabsorption in distal tubule, decreases phosphate reabsorption, stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make active vitamin D (calcitriol); effects in small intestine via calcitriol (Khan, Jose & Sharma, StatPearls 'Physiology, Parathyroid Hormone' 2022). Ivar Sandström, a young medical student at the Anatomical Department in Uppsala, discovered the glands in 1877, published 1879-80 'On a new gland in man and several mammals' (Johansson, Ups J Med Sci 2015). Collip 1925 extracted a parathyroid hormone that controls tetany and regulates blood calcium (J Biol Chem 1925;63:395); complete removal of parathyroids caused fatal tetany, proving them essential for life; Collip also remembered for his role in insulin (Kalra et al., Indian J Endocrinol Metab 2013).

cards.html:
Your neck

Four tiny glands run your blood calcium.

Meet PTH, parathyroid hormone.

Where

Behind your thyroid.

4 small glands sit at the back of the thyroid.

84
amino acids in one PTH peptide

The trigger

A calcium alarm.

Blood calcium drops
↓
PTH is released
↓
Calcium back up: PTH stops

3 jobs

Calcium from 3 places.

Bone
Releases stored calcium
Kidney
Keeps calcium. Lets phosphate go.
Gut
Absorbs more, via active vitamin D

Discovery

1877

A medical student in Uppsala, Sweden, first describes the glands.

1925

James Collip extracts the hormone. He also helped purify insulin.

Save this for your physiology exam.

Sources in the caption.
